  1          Plaintiffs Daniel Varady, Daniel Gruber, and Karen Schreiman, individually and on

 2   behalf of all others similarly situated, allege the following based on their personal experience

 3   and their counsel’s investigation:

 4                                        I. NATURE OF ACTION

 5          1.      This proposed class action suit against Defendants Wells Fargo & Company and

 6   Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC, d/b/a Wells Fargo Advisors (collectively, “Wells Fargo” or

 7   “Defendants”) arises out of Wells Fargo’s actions and conduct with respect to the cash sweep

 8   program it operates.

 9          2.      Wells Fargo automatically enrolls retail customers with uninvested cash in their

10   brokerage accounts in what is known as a “cash sweep” account. The Wells Fargo cash sweep

11   accounts at issue in this case are the Wells Fargo Standard Bank Deposit Sweep and the Wells

12   Fargo Expanded Deposit Sweep (collectively, the “Wells Fargo Sweep Program”). The program

13   was designed, created, and developed by Wells Fargo and it does not provide any other types of

14   sweep vehicles for its retail customers’ uninvested cash.

15          3.      Plaintiffs and Class members are retail customers with advisory (or discretionary)

16   and self-managed (non-discretionary) brokerage accounts, including retirement accounts, with

17   Wells Fargo. Plaintiffs and Class members’ uninvested cash was automatically swept into

18   interest-bearing accounts with Wells Fargo affiliated banks, pursuant to the Wells Fargo Sweep

19   Program. At all relevant times, Wells Fargo had legal and/or contractual duties to Plaintiffs and

20   the proposed Class to obtain reasonable rates on their uninvested cash.

21          4.      In operating the Wells Fargo Sweep Program, however, Wells Fargo breached its

22   legal and/or contractual duties to Plaintiffs and Class members. Wells Fargo caused Plaintiffs’

23   and Class members’ uninvested cash to be deposited with program banks that pay unreasonable

24   rates of return, sometimes as low as .02%, but paid Wells Fargo significant and higher fees at the

25   expense of Wells Fargo customers. In contrast, Wells Fargo competitors paid interest rates as

26   high as 5%. As a result of its practices, Wells Fargo generated massive revenues for itself while

27   paying its customers a pittance.

28

                            FIRST AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 3   breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, gross negligence, breach of the implied covenant of

 4   good faith and fair dealing, and unjust enrichment. Plaintiffs seek all available monetary and

 5   equitable relief, including damages, restitution, an injunction, and all other appropriate relief.

 6                                            II.     PARTIES

 9           8.     Plaintiff Karen Schreiman is a resident and citizen of Redondo Beach, California.

12   Company is a leading financial services company with assets of approximately $1.9 trillion and

13   office locations around the world. Wells Fargo & Company touts itself as a company that “proudly

14   serves consumers” and “partners with our customers to help them achieve their financial goals[.]”

15   Wells Fargo is named as a defendant in its capacity as the parent company and control person of

16   Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC, dba Wells Fargo Advisors.

17           10.    Defendant Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC, dba Wells Fargo Advisors is a

18   Delaware corporation, headquartered at One North Jefferson Avenue, St. Louis, Missouri 63103.

19   Wells Fargo Advisors is a dually registered broker-dealer and registered investment advisor that

20   offers brokerage and investment advisory services to its nationwide client base. Wells Fargo

21   Advisors is a trade name used by Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC. Wells Fargo Advisors

22   provides brokerage services to Plaintiffs and Class members, acting as its customers’ agent

23   regarding the establishment, maintenance, and operation of the Wells Fargo Sweep Program. Wells

24   Fargo Clearing Services, LLC is a majority-owned subsidiary of Defendant Wells Fargo &

25   Company. In BrokerCheck reports filed with the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority

 2          11.     This Court has jurisdiction over this action under the Class Action Fairness

 3   Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d). There are at least one hundred members in the proposed class, the

 4   aggregated claims of the individual class members exceed the sum or value of $5,000,000,

 6   proposed Class, including Plaintiffs, are citizens of a state different from Defendants. The Court

 7   has supplemental jurisdiction over the alleged state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 because

 8   they form part of the same case or controversy.

 9          12.     This Court may exercise jurisdiction over Defendants because at least one

11   and intentionally avail themselves of the markets within this District through the promotion, sale,

12   and marketing of their services, thus rendering the exercise of jurisdiction by this Court proper and

13   necessary.

14          13.     Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391 because at least one

15   Defendant resides in this District and a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to

16   Plaintiffs’ claims emanated from this District.

18          14.     New York law governs Plaintiffs’ and Class members’ claims by virtue of the choice

19   of law provision selecting New York law in the General Account Agreement and Disclosure

21                                  V.        FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

22                            A.          Background on Cash Sweep Accounts

23          15.     A “cash sweep” or “sweep” account is typically linked to a brokerage account and

24   holds uninvested money, such as the initial cash deposits into a brokerage account before the cash

25   is invested in a security or cash customers prefer to remain uninvested. The uninvested cash is

                           FIRST AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
  1   “swept” into an interest-bearing account to ensure that the cash is not sitting idly not generating

 2   income.

 3          16.     Today, cash sweep programs work by automatically “sweeping” uninvested cash

 4   each day into one or more banks that are usually affiliated with the brokerage firm. Historically,

 5   uninvested client cash sat with brokerage firms on their balance sheets, but in the 1960s, brokerage

 6   firms started depositing the cash with banks in the form of certificates of deposit. In early 2000,

 7   Merrill Lynch began offering the type of sweep accounts or programs that are available today and

 8   later other brokerage firms, like Charles Schwab, did the same.

 9          17.     The Security and Exchanges Commission (“SEC”) defines a sweep program as a

10   “service provided by a broker or dealer where it offers to its customers the option to automatically

11   transfer free credit balances in the securities account of the customer to either a money market

12   mutual fund product . . . or an account at a bank whose deposits are insured by the Federal Deposit

13   Insurance Corporation.” 17 C.F.R. 240.15c3-3(a)(17).

14          18.     Brokerages like Wells Fargo have significant discretion in the creation of their cash

15   sweep programs. For example, they can create money market funds as the sweep vehicles for their

16   customers’ uninvested cash. They also have discretion regarding the banks that they partner with.

17          19.     Brokerage firms collectively hold around $1 trillion dollars at any given time in

18   uninvested cash. The amount of uninvested client cash that Wells Fargo holds is not publicly

19   available, but Wells Fargo reported approximately $100 billion in total deposits from its Wealth

20   and Investment Management division in Q2 2024 and earnings of over $900 million in net interest

21   income.2

22          20.     Brokerage firms and affiliated banks earn significant net interest income (or

23   “spread”)—that is, the difference between the rate of interest earned by custodians loaning and

24   investing the sweep deposits and the interest paid to brokerage customers.

25          21.     The amount of money that brokerage firms earn under their sweep programs are

26   based on their agreements with the banks they partner with to run their cash sweep programs. The

 3          28.     As described in Part C below, brokerage firms owe a fiduciary duty to act in the

 4   best interests of their customers, including with respect to their clients’ uninvested cash holdings.

 5                             B.      Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Program

 6          29.     Wells Fargo designed and developed the Wells Fargo Sweep Program in a manner

 7   that puts its financial interests above that of Wells Fargo customers and generates massive

 8   revenues for itself at the expense of Wells Fargo customers. Wells Fargo had discretion in how to

 9   structure and implement the Wells Fargo Sweep Program.

10          30.     For example, Wells Fargo could have created a money market fund as a cash sweep

11   vehicle for Wells Fargo’s retail customers’ uninvested cash. In fact, it has such an option for its

12   institutional clients—such as government agencies, municipalities, or insurance and mutual fund

13   companies.5 Unlike some of its competitors, Wells Fargo does not provide an alternative sweep

14   avenue beyond depositing its retail customers’ uninvested cash into low interest-bearing deposit

15   accounts with banks affiliated with the Wells Fargo Sweep Program.6

16          31.     Under the program currently, Wells Fargo automatically assigns all its retail

17   customers to one of two different cash sweep accounts by default based on the type of account the

18   customer has. The first program is the Wells Fargo Standard Bank Deposit Sweep (“SBDS) for

19   resource and retirement accounts in Wells Fargo’s discretionary advisory program, and the second

20   program is the Wells Fargo Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep (“EBDS”), which is the default option

21   for new investment accounts (collectively referred to as the “Wells Fargo Sweep Program”).

22          32.     There are generally two types of Wells Fargo customers, advisory clients and self-

23   managed clients. Advisory clients are clients with brokerage accounts managed by Wells Fargo;

24   that is, Wells Fargo makes the decision on what stocks to buy and sell, while self-managed
